verdict.justification: Both deliverables use the correct combined MIG demand and recommend six days through week 13, five days in weeks 14–15, and regular time from week 16. A is preferable because it explicitly identifies sustained catch-up at the end of week 11, quantifies the week-10 shortfall, and gives management an actionable choice between temporary qualified support and an agreed schedule change. Its 60-hour buffer target also consistently explains retaining six days through week 13, whereas B claims its 30-hour step-down test is first met at week 13 even though the projected five-day schedule would satisfy that test from the end of week 12. B additionally says the transition builds the buffer to approximately 90 hours, but the supplied demand and proposed schedule produce approximately 116 hours by the end of week 15. More seriously, B incorrectly assures the reader that the dates still hold without pull-forward, despite week 13 demand exceeding maximum weekly capacity and therefore requiring advance production to avoid renewed past due. A's email is longer than the requested few sentences and should be shortened, but its clearer exception handling, consistent buffer rationale, and quantified consequences of immediate day reductions make it the stronger managerial deliverable.
